chapter.title: What counts as a good argument

cards.body: Socrates never wrote a word, and Athens executed him for asking questions. Western philosophy is one dinner-table argument that has run for about 2,500 years, and he was the guest who kept turning to whoever had just spoken and asking *why*. An opinion is only a seat at that table. **A claim plus the reasons that hold it up is an argument**, and that is what earns you a hearing.
cards.simpler: Socrates never wrote anything down, and the city of Athens put him to death for asking questions. Western philosophy is like one long dinner-table argument that has lasted about 2,500 years. Socrates was the guest who kept asking whoever had just spoken why they believed it. Having an opinion only gets you a seat at that table. **A claim plus the reasons that hold it up is an argument**, and that is what earns you a hearing.

cards.prompt: At dinner your cousin Dev says: 'Pineapple on pizza is a crime. I've hated it since I was 6.' Which part is the claim, the thing he wants you to accept?

options.text: Both sentences are claims; there is no reason here

whyNot.b: That's the reason, not the claim: it's the fact Dev holds up to back the verdict, not the verdict itself.
whyNot.c: That's two sentences, not two claims: the second one has a job, trying to hold the first one up. Whether it manages is a separate question.

cards.reteach: The claim is the sentence someone wants you to walk away believing. The reason is whatever they point at when you say 'why?'. Dev wants you to believe pineapple pizza is a crime, and his 6-year-old self is the evidence he offers.

cards.title: Two parts, every time
cards.body:
Every opinion worth arguing about has two parts. The *claim* is the sentence someone wants you to agree with. The *reasons* are what they say when you ask why.

You'd think the hard part is finding the reasons. It isn't. People hand you reasons all day, on buses, in group chats, across tables. The hard part is noticing **whether the reasons are actually touching the claim**, or just sitting next to it on the plate.

Try it on the next advert you see. Underline the claim. Circle what's offered as 'because'. Often there is nothing to circle.
cards.simpler: Every opinion has two parts. The claim is the sentence someone wants you to agree with. The reasons are what they say when you ask why. Finding reasons is easy. People give them all day, on buses and in group chats. The hard part is noticing **whether the reasons actually touch the claim** or sit next to it. Try this with the next advert you see. Underline the claim. Circle the because. Often there is nothing to circle.

cards.title: Priya and the 12%
cards.body: Priya's landlord emails: 'Rent goes up 12% in March. Everyone's rent is going up.' The claim is that her rent should rise 12%. The reason is that everyone's is rising. She writes back one line: 'Whose rent, and by how much?' Two days of silence, then a reply offering 8%. **The reason was true and still didn't carry the number.**
cards.simpler: Priya's landlord sends an email. Rent goes up 12% in March, it says, because everyone's rent is going up. The claim is that her rent should rise 12%. The reason is that everyone's rent is rising. She writes back one line: whose rent, and by how much? Two days of silence. Then a reply offering 8%. **The reason was true and still did not carry the number.**

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'This phone is the best one you can buy. It's the one I have.' Does her reason hold up her claim?

options.text: Yes: owning it means she knows it's good
No: the reason tells you what she bought, not whether it's the best
Yes, as long as she's happy with it

whyNot.a: That's familiarity, not support: knowing one phone well tells you about that phone, not how it ranks against the ones she has never used.
whyNot.c: That's a different claim: 'I'm happy with mine' would be held up by her being happy. 'Best you can buy' needs a comparison, and none was offered.

cards.reteach: Ask one question: if the reason is completely true, does the claim have to follow? She really does own that phone. 'Best you can buy' still doesn't follow, because 'best' is a comparison and she compared it with nothing.

cards.title: The test: grant it, then ask
cards.body:
Here is the one test. **Grant the reason completely**, pretend it is 100% true, then ask: does the claim now have to be true? If yes, the reason holds. If the claim could still be false, the reason is decoration.

This is why a reason can be true and still useless. 'Everyone's rent is rising' was true. 'Therefore 12%' did not follow. Picture the reason as a bolt. A solid bolt fitted to the wrong door keeps nothing shut.

So a good argument is not one with true-sounding reasons. It is one where the reasons, once granted, leave the claim nowhere to hide.
cards.simpler: Here is the one test. **Grant the reason completely**, as if it were fully true, then ask whether the claim now has to be true. If yes, the reason holds. If the claim could still be false, the reason is only decoration. 'Everyone's rent is rising' was true. 'So 12%' did not follow. A strong bolt on the wrong door keeps nothing shut. Good reasons, once granted, leave the claim nowhere to hide.

cards.body: Marco posts that a new bike lane will cut traffic on his street. Someone replies: 'You don't even drive.' Marco spends an hour defending his licence, and nobody mentions traffic again. Spot it this way: **when the reply is about the person, not the claim**, the argument has left the table. Ask where the claim went.
cards.simpler: Marco posts that a new bike lane will cut traffic on his street. Someone replies that he does not even drive. Marco spends an hour defending his driving licence, and nobody mentions traffic again. Here is how to spot it: **when the reply is about the person, not the claim**, the argument has left the table. It is like answering a question about the food by talking about the cook. Ask where the claim went.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a complete argument: a claim with a reason that, if granted, holds it up?

options.text: 'We should leave at 7. The film starts at 7:30 and the drive takes 20 minutes.'
'We should leave at 7. I just feel it.'
'We should leave at 7. Last time we were late you blamed me.'

whyNot.b: That's a claim with a mood, not a reason: a feeling tells you about the speaker, not about when the film starts.
whyNot.c: That's a grievance, not a reason: who got blamed last time has no bearing on tonight's start time.

cards.reteach: Run the test. Grant that the film really starts at 7:30 and the drive really takes 20 minutes, and leaving at 7 follows. Grant the feeling, grant the old blame, and 7 still floats free, unsupported.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Every opinion is a claim plus reasons, and the only test that matters is this: **if the reasons were fully true, would the claim have to follow?** Most arguments fail that test with reasons that are perfectly true and beside the point.

Tomorrow: the man who would not stop asking why, and why Athens killed him.
cards.simpler: Every opinion is a claim plus reasons. The only test that matters is this: **if the reasons were fully true, would the claim have to follow?** Most arguments fail that test. Their reasons are perfectly true and still beside the point, like a correct answer to a different question. Tomorrow: the man who would not stop asking why, and why Athens killed him.

cards.body: Open your last group chat where someone had an opinion. Find the claim. Find the 'because'. Grant the 'because' fully and ask whether the claim follows. Reply with nothing. Just notice.
cards.simpler: Open the last group chat where someone shared an opinion. Find the claim, the thing they wanted everyone to agree with. Find the because, the reason they gave. Now **grant the because fully and ask whether the claim follows**. Do not reply. Do not correct anyone. Just notice what you see, the way you might notice a loose button without sewing it on.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now split any opinion into its claim and its reasons, and say whether the reasons hold it up.
